name: Hungary and Transylvania
hover_description: Hungary/Transylvania, c. 1700–1756: Late prosecution under Habsburg consolidation. Szeged burning 1728. Táltos tradition. Pócs and Klaniczay's primary territory.
panel_description:
Hungary and Transylvania produced a distinctive late prosecution pattern, with the most intensive witch trials occurring in the early eighteenth century — well after the main western European prosecution wave had ended — under the Habsburg consolidation of the region following the Ottoman withdrawal. The Szeged burning of 1728, in which approximately thirteen persons were executed for witchcraft, is the most-documented Hungarian mass prosecution.

  Eva Pócs's Between the Living and the Dead (1999) and Gábor Klaniczay's The Uses of Supernatural Power (1990) are the foundational English-language studies of Central European, and specifically Hungarian and Balkan, prosecution patterns. Their work is essential for understanding the táltos tradition — a Hungarian shaman-like figure whose spirit-battle tradition parallels the Friulian benandanti and the Sámi noaidi — which Ginzburg incorporates into his pan-Eurasian ecstatic-tradition thesis.

  The late timing of Hungarian prosecution (relative to western Europe) reflects the region's different political history: Ottoman occupation had disrupted normal ecclesiastical and secular court functioning, and the Habsburg legal integration of the reconquered territories in the 1690s-1700s brought with it prosecution frameworks that were already becoming obsolete in western Europe. Hungary thus serves as a kind of temporal experiment: prosecution occurring under the same ideological framework but in different political circumstances.

  Habsburg Empress Maria Theresa's decree of 1758 officially ended witch prosecution in the Habsburg territories, including Hungary, through a centralizing reform that required imperial review of all witchcraft convictions.
source_method: Hungarian state archives; analyzed in Pócs, Between the Living and the Dead (1999); Klaniczay, The Uses of Supernatural Power (1990); Hutton, The Witch (2017)
